task: This is a synthetic writing exercise. Using these fictional reporting notes, write a newspaper explainer for general readers answering the question: What is carbon capture, how does it work, and why is it controversial? Draw only on the supplied notes; do not invent additional reported events, scenes, or quotations. Write from this reporting snapshot as of April 8, 2025. Include a headline. Target 450 to 650 words. Follow AP style.

facts.text: Carbon capture and storage (CCS) refers to technologies that remove carbon dioxide from industrial emissions or the atmosphere and compress and store it underground.
Point-source capture installs equipment at a smokestacks — power plants, steel mills, cement factories — to remove CO2 before it enters the atmosphere; captured gas is typically 90% or more pure CO2.
The most common industrial capture method uses amine solvents that chemically absorb CO2 from flue gas; the CO2 is then released by heating the solvent, compressed, and sent to a storage site.

Compressed CO2 is injected into geological formations, typically depleted oil and gas reservoirs or deep saline aquifers, at depths of more than one kilometer where pressure keeps it in a supercritical state.

At supercritical pressure and temperature, CO2 behaves as a dense fluid rather than a gas and cannot escape unless the geological cap rock is breached; well-chosen sites are considered geologically stable for thousands of years.

Carbon economist Dr. Naomi Castillo of Westfield University said: "CCS has a legitimate engineering role in sectors like cement and steel where there is no practical alternative to combustion. The controversy is around using it to justify continued fossil fuel use in sectors where cleaner alternatives exist."
The energy penalty is a major limitation: capturing CO2 from a power plant's exhaust requires 15 to 25% more energy input per unit of electricity generated, increasing fuel consumption and cost.

Direct air capture (DAC) removes CO2 directly from ambient air rather than from concentrated industrial emissions; the CO2 concentration in air (about 420 parts per million) is far lower than in flue gas, making DAC more energy-intensive and expensive.
The current cost of DAC removal ranges from $300 to $1,000 per tonne of CO2; point-source capture from concentrated industrial emissions costs $50 to $150 per tonne.

The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change has concluded that meeting the 1.5-degree Celsius warming target almost certainly requires some carbon removal from the atmosphere, in addition to emissions cuts.

Critics argue that the scale of CCS needed to matter — billions of tonnes per year — has never been demonstrated, and that the technology has a history of cost overruns and operational delays at large facilities.

Bioenergy with carbon capture and storage (BECCS) combines growing biomass — which absorbs CO2 — with burning that biomass for energy and capturing the exhaust; in theory, it produces net-negative emissions.
Enhanced oil recovery uses injected CO2 to push more oil out of depleted reservoirs; some critics argue this practice subsidizes oil production rather than removing carbon.
Dr. Castillo said the engineering hurdles are surmountable but the economic hurdles are not without a carbon price or direct subsidy that makes capture cost-competitive with simply emitting.
The United States offers tax credits of $85 per tonne for geological CO2 storage and $60 per tonne for CO2 used in industrial processes.
The 45Q tax credit has attracted investment in large-scale CCS projects at industrial facilities; at least a dozen major projects are under development in North America.

Monitoring whether stored CO2 stays underground requires long-term seismic and geochemical monitoring; liability for stored CO2 over geological time scales is an unresolved legal question in most jurisdictions.
Leakage from poorly chosen or poorly sealed storage sites could release CO2 gradually, reducing the climate benefit; no large-scale storage site has experienced a confirmed breach.
Ocean storage of CO2 has been proposed but is not practiced; it would acidify local seawater and is banned by international ocean dumping treaties.
Dr. Castillo said a realistic accounting of CCS's role in climate policy must distinguish between proven point-source capture and aspirational claims for direct air capture at scale.

forbidden_additions: a claim that CCS has been proven at the scale needed for 1.5-degree pathways
a storage cost or DAC cost outside the ranges in the notes
a statement that no CCS projects exist
